title: Latitude & Longitude Basics
summary: Latitude = how far north/south of the equator; longitude = how far east/west of the Prime Meridian.
quick_actions: Latitude lines run east-west and measure 0° (equator) to 90° N or S at the poles.
Longitude lines run north-south (pole to pole) and measure 0° (Prime Meridian, through Greenwich, UK) to 180° E or W.
Coordinates are always written latitude first, then longitude (e.g. 40.7128° N, 74.0060° W).
A minus sign is a common shorthand for S or W (e.g. -74.0060 means 74.0060° W).
more_info: Every point on Earth's surface has a unique latitude/longitude pair - this is the basis every other coordinate format (DMS, UTM, MGRS) is built on or converts to/from.

title: Coordinate Formats (DD, DMS, UTM, MGRS)
summary: The same location can be written several different ways - know which one your device/map uses.
quick_actions: Decimal Degrees (DD): e.g. 38.5, -98.30 - the format most phone GPS apps show by default.
Degrees Minutes Seconds (DMS): e.g. 42°30'00" N, 98°15'30" W - each degree splits into 60 minutes, each minute into 60 seconds.
UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator): divides the world into 60 numbered zones, position given as an easting/northing in meters - common on USGS topographic maps.
MGRS (Military Grid Reference System): the same UTM grid, but identifies the 100km square with letters instead of numbers - common on military/tactical maps.
more_info: To convert DD to DMS: the whole number is degrees; multiply the decimal part by 60 for minutes; multiply the leftover decimal by 60 again for seconds. All formats describe the same underlying grid - they're just different notations for it.

title: How GPS Works Without Internet
summary: GPS gets your position from satellites directly - it never needed the internet or cell service.
quick_actions: A GPS receiver listens for timing signals broadcast by satellites - it doesn't send or receive anything over the internet or cell network to compute a position.
At least 4 satellites in view are needed for a full 3D position fix (latitude, longitude, and elevation).
The US maintains at least 24 operational GPS satellites at all times, so several are visible from almost anywhere on Earth at any time.
What DOES need the internet/cell data: downloading new map tiles, live traffic, or searching for an address by name - the position fix itself does not.
more_info: This is why a phone in airplane mode (with GPS/location services left on) can still show your coordinates and a pre-downloaded map with no signal at all - only fetching new map data or looking up a place by name requires connectivity.

title: Cardinal Directions & Compass Bearings
summary: N/E/S/W at 90° intervals; a bearing is the clockwise angle from north to your target.
quick_actions: Cardinal directions: North 0°, East 90°, South 180°, West 270°.
Intercardinal directions sit halfway between: Northeast 45°, Southeast 135°, Southwest 225°, Northwest 315°.
A compass bearing is the clockwise angle from north to wherever you're pointing/heading.

Check current magnetic declination for your area (ngdc.noaa.gov/geomag) before navigating by compass bearing - a map's 'true north' and a compass's 'magnetic north' can differ enough to send you well off course.
more_info: Magnetic declination varies by location and changes slowly over time, so a fixed number memorized once can become inaccurate years later - check it for your actual area when it matters.

title: Basic Offline Navigation Concepts
summary: A paper map, a compass, and knowing your last confirmed position go a long way with zero electronics.
quick_actions: Orient the map: align it so north on the paper points to actual north (using a compass, or the sun near local noon in the Northern Hemisphere as a rough check).

Dead reckoning: estimate your current position from a known starting point plus the direction and distance you've traveled since - simple, but errors add up the longer you go without checking a landmark.
Use terrain/landmarks (a distinct hill, river bend, or intersection) to confirm your estimated position whenever you can - don't rely on dead reckoning alone for long stretches.

A GPS device or phone (see How GPS Works Without Internet) can give you an exact coordinate to place on a paper map even with zero cell/Wi-Fi signal, combining the reliability of electronics with the resilience of paper.
more_info: None of this requires memorizing survival techniques - the practical takeaway is: carry a paper map of your area as a backup, know roughly how to read it, and treat GPS coordinates and paper maps as complementary, not either/or.

title: Map Scale
summary: A representative fraction like 1:24,000 means 1 unit on the map equals 24,000 of the same unit on the ground.
quick_actions: Representative fraction (e.g. 1:24,000): 1 inch on the map = 24,000 inches on the ground (about 2,000 feet, or roughly 0.38 miles).
A bar/graphic scale (a ruler-like line marked in real-world distances printed on the map) stays accurate even if the map is photocopied, scanned, or resized - a text fraction does not.

'Large scale' = more detail over a smaller area (e.g. 1:24,000 city/local map). 'Small scale' = less detail over a bigger area (e.g. 1:1,000,000 whole-country map) - counterintuitively, the bigger the second number, the smaller the scale.
USGS 7.5-minute topographic quadrangles (the standard detailed US topo series) are 1:24,000.
more_info: Always prefer the printed bar scale over a remembered representative fraction when measuring distance on an actual paper map - if the map was ever resized (photocopied, printed at a different size, or is a screen capture), the text fraction is now wrong but a bar scale printed on the same page resizes right along with it.

title: Reading Contour Lines
summary: Each contour line connects points of equal elevation - spacing and shape tell you the terrain's steepness and form.
quick_actions: Each contour line connects points of equal elevation - walk exactly along one and you neither climb nor descend.
Lines close together = steep terrain. Lines spread far apart = gentle or flat terrain.

A closed loop by itself = a hilltop/high point. The same loop with short tick marks (hachures) pointing inward = a depression or sinkhole, not a hill - the hachures are the only thing that tells them apart.
Every 4th or 5th line is usually a heavier, labeled 'index contour.' Count the lighter lines between two index contours and multiply by the map's stated contour interval to read an exact elevation.
more_info: This covers the core reading skill; the full official legend for every contour/elevation symbol variation (glaciers, cliffs, benchmarks, and more) is retained in full in the Document Library as an original USGS publication - see the cross-link below.

title: True North vs. Magnetic North
summary: A map's grid points to true (geographic) north; a compass needle points to magnetic north - the angle between them is declination.
quick_actions: True north points along the Earth's surface toward the geographic North Pole - this is what a map's grid lines and printed 'up' are drawn to.
Magnetic north is the direction a compass needle actually points, toward the wandering magnetic north pole - it is NOT the same point, and the difference is called magnetic declination.

Declination varies by location (it can be 0°, or over 15° in parts of the US) and drifts slowly over years, so a number memorized long ago can become noticeably wrong - check current declination for the actual area (ngdc.noaa.gov/geomag) when it matters.

USGS topographic maps print a small declination diagram in the margin showing the exact angle for that specific map's location and print date - use the map's own printed diagram over a memorized figure whenever one is available.
more_info: To convert a compass (magnetic) bearing to a true bearing: add easterly declination, subtract westerly declination. Mnemonics for this exist ('east is least, west is best' and others) but are easy to misremember backwards - when it matters, work it out from the actual declination diagram rather than trusting a half-remembered rhyme.

title: United States Time Zones
summary: 9 official US time zones exist under the Uniform Time Act - not all of them observe daylight saving time.
quick_actions: The Uniform Time Act establishes 9 official US time zones: Atlantic, Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific, Alaska, Hawaii-Aleutian, Samoa, and Chamorro.
Daylight saving time is NOT observed in: Arizona (except the Navajo Nation, which does observe it), Hawaii, American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, and the US Virgin Islands.
Time zone boundaries follow a federal process (petitioned through the US Department of Transportation), not state lines - a handful of counties sit in a different zone than the rest of their state.

title: World Time Zones: UTC Reference Points
summary: A selection of reference points across the UTC range - not a complete list of every zone.
quick_actions: Time zones are expressed as an offset from UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, the modern successor to GMT) - UTC+0 at Greenwich, increasing eastward, decreasing westward.
Not every zone is a whole hour: India is UTC+5:30 and Nepal is UTC+5:45 - always check the minutes, not just the hour, for these.
The International Date Line (roughly, but not exactly, the 180° meridian) is where the calendar day changes - crossing it westward skips a day forward, crossing it eastward repeats a day.
